newsitem.title: USA: U.S. in new 'open skies' efforts in Asia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. in new 'open skies' efforts in Asia.

text.p: A senior U.S. Transportation Department official said Thursday the United States would put new emphasis next year on reaching "open skies" accords in the many closed aviation markets of Asia.
"I look forward to good news on this front in a period of months, certainly, rather than years," he said.

Mark Gerchick, deputy assistant secretary for aviation and international affairs, said that after recent successes in Europe, efforts would now go to reach accords with smaller Asian nations. He added, however, that Japan was the prize.

The open market agreements reached with smaller European countries led to the "open skies" pact with Germany, officials say, and played a role in the talks now underway with Britain and wider discussions with the European Union.
Efforts to remove aviation restrictions also were underway with France and Portugal.
Gerchick, who addressed the North American section of the Airports Council International, an airports trade group, made no comment on the progress of the current British talks.
He restated the U.S. position that nothing short of a full free market accord, with the opening of London's Heathrow airport to additional American flights, would be acceptable.
Gerchick said Asia was the world's fastest-growing aviation market, and Japan the key, but Washington has not yet been able to negotiate an "open skies" pact with Tokyo.

Gerchick said talks were underway with Malaysia, Taiwan, South Korea, Singapore and New Zealand and was optimistic of getting results to form the critical mass needed to persaude bigger nations drop their aviation barriers.

He said a study showed that Japan was greatly underserved by international air services and that new routes have a major impact on domestic growth. He said, three new airlines have recently started up in Japan to fill the void.
"This is bound to have an impact on the thinking of regulators in Japan," Gerchick said.
Answering questions, he said the administration was looking into easing the law limiting foreign ownership of U.S. airlines to 25 percent.
Congress has long opposed relaxing the limitation.
